If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. In Newark rent-controlled units, rent may not rise more than the allowed percentage in any 12-month period, and never more than 4%, even if tenants or owners change. No increase is allowed if the building is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered the unit, so check the registration with the Office of Rent Control.

May apply (the building's age is not in the data). If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. It only applies if the owner filed the required notice, which public data can't show.

A0312.explanation: Pending proposal, not law. It would cover this address if enacted. This Massachusetts bill would address algorithmic rent fixing in rental housing, but it is not law. It was reported favorably by the Joint Committee on Housing on 3/12/2026 and referred to House Ways and Means, so renters have no new rights under it yet.

Pending proposal, not law. It would cover this address if enacted. A Massachusetts bill would ban algorithmic rent setting, but it is not law. As of the latest action it was referred to the Senate Committee on Ways and Means, so it gives renters no rights yet.

Applies. In Massachusetts, a rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who originally hired and contracted with the broker. If the landlord hired the broker, you as a tenant cannot be made to pay that fee.

Applies. At or before move-in, a landlord or the landlord's agent can only require you to pay first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of up to one month's rent, and the cost of a new lock and key. Since August 1, 2025, this also bars requiring you to pay the landlord's agent (such as the landlord's broker) anything beyond those items.

Applies. A landlord who threatens or takes reprisals (including eviction notices, rent increases or changed lease terms) because you complained about code violations, took legal action, or joined a tenants' union owes you at least one to three months' rent or your actual damages plus attorney's fees. A termination notice (other than for nonpayment), rent increase or substantial change in terms within six months after such activity is presumed to be retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence.

Applies. Massachusetts cities and towns generally cannot enact, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no local rent cap to rely on. The only exception is a voluntary program for owners of 10 or more units with fair market rent of $400 or less, where the city pays owners the difference from its general funds.

Applies. A Massachusetts landlord may not refuse to rent to you or otherwise discriminate against you because you receive public assistance or a housing subsidy such as a rental voucher, or because of that program's requirements. Ads may not state a preference against public assistance recipients.

Applies. Your landlord cannot charge a security deposit larger than one month's rent, must put it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and must give you a signed statement of the apartment's condition. If the state housing office issues regulations, a landlord may offer an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, and deposit plus fees can never exceed one month's rent in total. Your landlord must return your security deposit, minus only unpaid rent/water charges, allowed tax escalation, or documented damage beyond normal wear and tear, within 30 days after you move out, and must pay you yearly interest on it. If the landlord fails to return it on time, you can sue for three times the amount owed plus court costs and attorney's fees.

Applies. Any Boston landlord planning to end your tenancy must give you a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources together with the Notice to Quit or non-renewal notice; if you didn't get it, report it to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity (617-635-2500 or 311). A violation does not stop the eviction process. Note: Notice requirement only; Boston, MA has no just-cause eviction law.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you apply to housing funded by Boston DND or an income-restricted inclusionary unit, the provider cannot use a blanket ban on people with records and may not consider arrests without conviction, sealed or expunged convictions, juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old. If you are denied because of a conviction, ask for case-by-case review and offer evidence of rehabilitation. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the housing provider receives DND funding or land; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is an income-restricted unit under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.)

Applies. In Boston, a landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because you use rental assistance such as a Section 8, social security disability or veterans voucher. If a landlord says they don't accept vouchers, you can file a complaint with the Boston Fair Housing Commission.

A0313.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site.

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

May apply (the building's age is not in the data). If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. It only applies if the owner filed the required notice, which public data can't show.

A0314.explanation: Applies. Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

Applies. A landlord may charge an application screening fee no higher than the actual out-of-pocket cost of screening you, and never more than $30 per applicant, adjusted annually for CPI increases since 1998. Ask for the current CPI-adjusted figure if you are charged more than $30. A landlord may not charge you a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A landlord may charge a screening fee only if they either consider complete applications in order received under written criteria (approving the first qualified applicant and charging only when your application is actually considered, refunding within 7 days if collected by mistake), or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever is first. The landlord must give you an itemized receipt (in person, by mail, or by email if agreed) showing out-of-pocket costs and time spent, and must return any part of the fee not used if no reference check or credit report was obtained. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your consumer credit report within seven days of receiving it, by personal delivery, mail, or email.

Covered, but superseded here: No eviction for nonpayment unless arrears exceed Fair Market Rent (L.A. Mun. Code §§ 151.09(A)(1), 165.03(A) (Ord. No. 187763)) governs this address. Once all tenants have lawfully lived in the unit for 12 months (or at least one tenant for 24 months), your landlord may evict only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written termination notice. For a curable lease violation, the landlord must first give you a notice and a chance to fix it. If your landlord ends a covered tenancy for a no-fault reason (owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel), they must either pay you one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 calendar days of the notice or waive your final month's rent in writing. The notice must tell you about this right; if the landlord does not strictly comply, the notice is void.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).) Note: Stated on a city agency's page (Los Angeles, CA), not in the state's own text; check the figure against an official state source.

Covered, but superseded here: Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) annual allowable rent increase (L.A. Mun. Code § 151.06 (annual increase, as amended by Ord. No. 188795), § 151.02 (Rent Stabilization Ordinance)) governs this address. For a covered unit, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus local CPI, or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, measured from the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months. If you stay in the unit, the rent can be raised no more than twice in 12 months, and the landlord can set any starting rent for a new tenancy.

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. In an RSO unit, your landlord can evict only for a listed reason. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, lease violations, nuisance, or illegal use. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, a resident manager, demolition, a government order, or conversion to affordable housing. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict, give 30- or 60-day notice (sometimes 120 days), and pay relocation assistance. All termination notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days. (built 1919, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for a no-fault reason (owner or relative move-in, demolition or removal from rental use, government order to vacate, conversion, and similar), the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. The landlord must also pay you relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice; the 2026-27 amounts run from $11,000 to $27,400 depending on your tenancy length, income, age, disability or children. If you are not paid, you can raise the non-payment as a defense to the eviction and file a complaint with LAHD. (7 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.) Note: Bulletin A says a copy of the termination notice must be filed with LAHD no later than 3 days after service, while Bulletin B says within 3 business days. The fee chart in Bulletin B is labeled effective July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, while Bulletin A labels the same fees July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027.

Applies. If you rent in Los Angeles in a unit not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance and have lived there at least six months (or your original lease has expired), your landlord can evict you only for a listed at-fault or no-fault reason. For no-fault reasons, such as an owner move-in, demolition or removal from the rental market, the landlord may have to pay you relocation assistance.
Applies. In Los Angeles RSO and JCO units, your landlord cannot evict you for falling behind on rent unless you owe more than one month's Fair Market Rent for your unit's bedroom size.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your unit is a Protected Unit (this includes all RSO units) and is being demolished for new construction, you are entitled to at least the RSO/JCO relocation amount. If your household is lower income, you get the higher RPO or state amounts, up to $115,480 for extremely low income households under the City's standardized option. RPO protections also include a 6-month notice, a right to stay until 6 months before construction starts, a right to return if demolition does not proceed, and for some tenants a right of first refusal in the new building. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether a non-RSO unit is a Protected Unit (affordability covenant, occupancy by lower-income households within 5 years, or Ellis withdrawal within 10 years); Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower) for enhanced payments.)

Applies. If your LA unit was first built on or before October 1, 1978, your landlord may raise rent only once every 12 months, by no more than the city's published allowable percentage. Since February 2, 2026, landlords cannot add an extra percentage for utilities or a 10% increase for an added dependent. Increases beyond this, such as for capital improvements, need LAHD approval. (built 1919, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.) Note: D042: Sources disagree: status in_force; effective date 2025-07-01 / 2026-02-02.

Applies. If you rent an RSO unit in Los Angeles (certificate of occupancy first issued before October 1, 1978) and your landlord has held your deposit for at least a year, the landlord must pay you interest (3.03% for 2026, or the actual interest earned with a bank statement), as a direct payment or rent credit, and any unpaid interest when you move out. If unpaid, you can sue, including in Small Claims Court; the city will not investigate. (built 1919, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed. (8 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. In San Diego, a landlord may not use rent-setting software that uses nonpublic data from two or more landlords to set rents or occupancy levels, and no one may sell or license such software to landlords. A tenant can sue for an injunction, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees if the tenant wins.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Your landlord cannot end your tenancy without a listed at-fault cause (such as nonpayment, a lease breach not cured after written notice, nuisance, or criminal activity) or a good-faith no-fault cause (owner or family move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order to vacate, or demolition or substantial remodel). A no-fault notice must state the cause and give 30 or 60 days' notice under Civil Code 1946.1, and a notice that does not strictly comply is void. (8 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your landlord ends your tenancy for a no-fault reason, they must pay you two months of your current rent (three months if you are a senior aged 62 or older, or disabled), regardless of your income or length of tenancy. The landlord may instead waive the same amount of rent, and must pay a direct payment within 15 days of the notice. (8 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A San Diego landlord may not refuse to rent or renew, end a tenancy, falsely say a unit is unavailable, or advertise a preference based on your source of income, which includes Section 8 and other rental, deposit, or homeless assistance. Any income standard must count all of your income, including assistance, plus the combined income of co-tenants and cosigners.

A0317.explanation: Applies. Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

Applies. A landlord may charge an application screening fee no higher than the actual out-of-pocket cost of screening you, and never more than $30 per applicant, adjusted annually for CPI increases since 1998. Ask for the current CPI-adjusted figure if you are charged more than $30. A landlord may not charge you a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A landlord may charge a screening fee only if they either consider complete applications in order received under written criteria (approving the first qualified applicant and charging only when your application is actually considered, refunding within 7 days if collected by mistake), or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever is first. The landlord must give you an itemized receipt (in person, by mail, or by email if agreed) showing out-of-pocket costs and time spent, and must return any part of the fee not used if no reference check or credit report was obtained. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your consumer credit report within seven days of receiving it, by personal delivery, mail, or email.

Superseded here: Nonpayment eviction requires debt of at least one month's Fair Market Rent (Berkeley Mun. Code § 13.76.130(A)(1) (Ord. No. 7,950-N.S., Berkeley Tenant Protection and Right to Organize Act, approved by voters Nov. 5, 2024)) governs this address, whether or not the state rule would otherwise cover this unit. Once all tenants have lawfully lived in the unit for 12 months (or at least one tenant for 24 months), your landlord may evict only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written termination notice. For a curable lease violation, the landlord must first give you a notice and a chance to fix it. If your landlord ends a covered tenancy for a no-fault reason (owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel), they must either pay you one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 calendar days of the notice or waive your final month's rent in writing. The notice must tell you about this right; if the landlord does not strictly comply, the notice is void.

Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).) May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. For a covered unit, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus local CPI, or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, measured from the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months. If you stay in the unit, the rent can be raised no more than twice in 12 months, and the landlord can set any starting rent for a new tenancy. (at least 5 units, from the land-use description "Alameda County use code (5+ units)", so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history. (at least 5 units, from the land-use description "Alameda County use code (5+ units)", so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If a Berkeley landlord charges an application or credit-report fee, they must give you, in the application or a separate disclosure before taking the fee, a Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement and the maximum fee allowed under Civil Code 1950.6(b).
Applies. A Berkeley landlord cannot charge an existing tenant a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy or to add, replace, or remove a roommate. Lease terms to the contrary are unenforceable.

Applies. If your landlord evicts you to take the property off the rental market under the Ellis Act, they must pay you relocation assistance. Starting January 1, 2026, the standard payment is $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households.

Applies. May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. For 2026, eligible Berkeley landlords may raise a covered unit's rent ceiling by no more than 1.0%, and not before January 1, 2026. (at least 5 units, from the land-use description "Alameda County use code (5+ units)", so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If your unit is fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, your landlord must pay you interest on your security deposit at the end of each year. If you move out before year-end, you are owed a prorated amount.

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (6 units, from the assessor class code "4F-6U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (6 units, from the assessor class code "4F-6U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (6 units, from the assessor class code "4F-6U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Even after a conditional offer, a New Jersey landlord may never consider arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (6 units, from the assessor class code "4F-6U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (6 units, from the assessor class code "4F-6U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Hoboken landlords may not use software, algorithms or data-sharing platforms that use nonpublic competitor information (under 365 days old) to coordinate, recommend or set rents, lease terms or occupancy levels. If you believe your landlord is doing this, you or the Division of Housing can bring a complaint in Hoboken Municipal Court. Note: Ordinance title adds new Section 158-2 to Chapter 158, but the body heading numbers the section § 154-8; codified section number should be verified. Flag for review: from 2027-07-01, possible conflict with Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act – ban on algorithmic rent coordination (N.J.S.A. 56:9-20 to 56:9-26 (P.L. 2026, c.43; A3497 ACS 1R)).

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. When a registered rent-controlled unit is voluntarily vacated, the landlord may raise the rent for the next tenant by no more than 25% over the last rent paid, excluding any capital improvement surcharge. After that, later increases for the new tenant are again subject to Hoboken rent control, using the new rent as the base rent.

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. A landlord may use vacancy decontrol only if the tenant left voluntarily without harassment or pressure, was legally evicted, or left under a court order (not a holdover-only order). A tenant pressured out can ask the Rent Control Board for a hearing; the Board may rescind decontrol and restore the prior rent.

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. A Hoboken rent-controlled unit may be decontrolled at vacancy no more than once in any three-year period. If your unit got a vacancy increase within the past three years, a new vacancy increase is not allowed.

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. When your lease ends or renews (or for a periodic tenancy), your Hoboken landlord may not raise the rent by more than 5% or the CPI change, whichever is less. Only one such increase is allowed in any 12-month period, regardless of tenant turnover.

May apply (the building's age is not in the data). If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. It only applies if the owner filed the required notice, which public data can't show.

A0321.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site. Flag for review: from 2027-07-01, may preempt Jersey City Code § 218-12 (Ord. 25-057, as amended by Ord. 25-076).

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (7 units, from the assessor class code "3S-F-D-7U-NH" (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (7 units, from the assessor class code "3S-F-D-7U-NH", so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (7 units, from the assessor class code "3S-F-D-7U-NH", so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Jersey City landlords and their agents may not pay for or contract with a 'service provider' that pools competitors' nonpublic rent, supply or occupancy data and uses software to recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy levels. Service providers may not facilitate agreements among landlords not to compete on rents, fees or other terms. Tenants can report suspected use to the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations or sue if harmed. Note: Ordinance text calls Chapter 218 both 'Multiple Dwellings' and 'Fees and Charges', and renumbers existing §§ 218-12 through 218-18; codified section number should be verified. Effective date is computed, not stated. Flag for review: from 2027-07-01, possible conflict with Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act – ban on algorithmic rent coordination (N.J.S.A. 56:9-20 to 56:9-26 (P.L. 2026, c.43; A3497 ACS 1R)).

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. If you rent in a Jersey City building with 5 or more units, your rent may be regulated under the city's Rent Control Ordinance. You can ask the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations about your building's status through SeeClickFix or file an Illegal Rent Petition if you think your rent is illegal.

May apply (the building's age is not in the data). If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. It only applies if the owner filed the required notice, which public data can't show.

A0322.explanation: Applies. Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

Applies. A landlord may charge an application screening fee no higher than the actual out-of-pocket cost of screening you, and never more than $30 per applicant, adjusted annually for CPI increases since 1998. Ask for the current CPI-adjusted figure if you are charged more than $30. A landlord may not charge you a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A landlord may charge a screening fee only if they either consider complete applications in order received under written criteria (approving the first qualified applicant and charging only when your application is actually considered, refunding within 7 days if collected by mistake), or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever is first. The landlord must give you an itemized receipt (in person, by mail, or by email if agreed) showing out-of-pocket costs and time spent, and must return any part of the fee not used if no reference check or credit report was obtained. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your consumer credit report within seven days of receiving it, by personal delivery, mail, or email.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Once all tenants have lawfully lived in the unit for 12 months (or at least one tenant for 24 months), your landlord may evict only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written termination notice. For a curable lease violation, the landlord must first give you a notice and a chance to fix it. If your landlord ends a covered tenancy for a no-fault reason (owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel), they must either pay you one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 calendar days of the notice or waive your final month's rent in writing. The notice must tell you about this right; if the landlord does not strictly comply, the notice is void. (31 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.) Note: State law displaces less-protective local just-cause ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 while yielding to earlier or more-protective local ordinances; local coverage must be checked.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).) Note: Stated on a city agency's page (Los Angeles, CA), not in the state's own text; check the figure against an official state source.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. For a covered unit, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus local CPI, or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, measured from the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months. If you stay in the unit, the rent can be raised no more than twice in 12 months, and the landlord can set any starting rent for a new tenancy. (31 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history. (31 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed. (31 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. In San Diego, a landlord may not use rent-setting software that uses nonpublic data from two or more landlords to set rents or occupancy levels, and no one may sell or license such software to landlords. A tenant can sue for an injunction, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees if the tenant wins.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Your landlord cannot end your tenancy without a listed at-fault cause (such as nonpayment, a lease breach not cured after written notice, nuisance, or criminal activity) or a good-faith no-fault cause (owner or family move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order to vacate, or demolition or substantial remodel). A no-fault notice must state the cause and give 30 or 60 days' notice under Civil Code 1946.1, and a notice that does not strictly comply is void. (31 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your landlord ends your tenancy for a no-fault reason, they must pay you two months of your current rent (three months if you are a senior aged 62 or older, or disabled), regardless of your income or length of tenancy. The landlord may instead waive the same amount of rent, and must pay a direct payment within 15 days of the notice. (31 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A San Diego landlord may not refuse to rent or renew, end a tenancy, falsely say a unit is unavailable, or advertise a preference based on your source of income, which includes Section 8 and other rental, deposit, or homeless assistance. Any income standard must count all of your income, including assistance, plus the combined income of co-tenants and cosigners.

Applies. In an RSO unit, your landlord can evict only for a listed reason. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, lease violations, nuisance, or illegal use. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, a resident manager, demolition, a government order, or conversion to affordable housing. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict, give 30- or 60-day notice (sometimes 120 days), and pay relocation assistance. All termination notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days. (built 1907, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for a no-fault reason (owner or relative move-in, demolition or removal from rental use, government order to vacate, conversion, and similar), the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. The landlord must also pay you relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice; the 2026-27 amounts run from $11,000 to $27,400 depending on your tenancy length, income, age, disability or children. If you are not paid, you can raise the non-payment as a defense to the eviction and file a complaint with LAHD. (5 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.) Note: Bulletin A says a copy of the termination notice must be filed with LAHD no later than 3 days after service, while Bulletin B says within 3 business days. The fee chart in Bulletin B is labeled effective July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, while Bulletin A labels the same fees July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027.

Applies. If you rent in Los Angeles in a unit not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance and have lived there at least six months (or your original lease has expired), your landlord can evict you only for a listed at-fault or no-fault reason. For no-fault reasons, such as an owner move-in, demolition or removal from the rental market, the landlord may have to pay you relocation assistance.
Applies. In Los Angeles RSO and JCO units, your landlord cannot evict you for falling behind on rent unless you owe more than one month's Fair Market Rent for your unit's bedroom size.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your unit is a Protected Unit (this includes all RSO units) and is being demolished for new construction, you are entitled to at least the RSO/JCO relocation amount. If your household is lower income, you get the higher RPO or state amounts, up to $115,480 for extremely low income households under the City's standardized option. RPO protections also include a 6-month notice, a right to stay until 6 months before construction starts, a right to return if demolition does not proceed, and for some tenants a right of first refusal in the new building. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether a non-RSO unit is a Protected Unit (affordability covenant, occupancy by lower-income households within 5 years, or Ellis withdrawal within 10 years); Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower) for enhanced payments.)

Applies. If your LA unit was first built on or before October 1, 1978, your landlord may raise rent only once every 12 months, by no more than the city's published allowable percentage. Since February 2, 2026, landlords cannot add an extra percentage for utilities or a 10% increase for an added dependent. Increases beyond this, such as for capital improvements, need LAHD approval. (built 1907, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.) Note: D042: Sources disagree: status in_force; effective date 2025-07-01 / 2026-02-02.

Applies. If you rent an RSO unit in Los Angeles (certificate of occupancy first issued before October 1, 1978) and your landlord has held your deposit for at least a year, the landlord must pay you interest (3.03% for 2026, or the actual interest earned with a bank statement), as a direct payment or rent credit, and any unpaid interest when you move out. If unpaid, you can sue, including in Small Claims Court; the city will not investigate. (built 1907, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed. (6 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Landlords in San Francisco may not use, and vendors may not sell, software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents or manage occupancy. If you believe a landlord or vendor is violating this, you (or the City Attorney) can bring a civil lawsuit.

Applies. A landlord can only evict you from a unit covered by the SF Rent Ordinance for one of 17 listed just causes, and that cause must be the landlord's dominant motive. A lease simply expiring or the building being sold is not a just cause, and a landlord also needs just cause to remove housing services such as parking, storage, or laundry.

Applies. If you are served an Ellis Act eviction notice between 3/1/26 and 2/28/27, you are owed $11,110.05 per tenant, up to $33,330.13 per unit. Each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant gets an additional $7,443.90.

Applies. If you are served an eviction notice between 3/1/26 and 2/28/27 for owner or relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation, you are owed $8,245 per tenant, up to $24,733 per unit. Each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant, or household with minor children, gets an additional $5,497.

Applies. If you live in a rent-controlled unit in San Francisco, your landlord's annual increase for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is limited to 1.6% of your base rent. For example, on a $2,000 base rent the increase is $32, for a new base rent of $2,032. (built 1885, before the 1979-06-13 cutoff.)

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are applying for affordable housing in San Francisco and have an arrest or conviction history, the Fair Chance Ordinance limits how that history can be used in the housing decision. You can contact the Human Rights Commission to file a complaint. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Unit must be affordable housing.)

A0325.explanation: Enacted, but takes effect 2027-07-01, after the 2026-10-01 query date. Landlords in New Jersey may not pay for or use rent-setting software or algorithmic devices that perform a 'coordinating function', meaning setting or recommending rents, lease terms or occupancy using competitors' nonpublic data. Anyone may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. If you suspect your landlord is doing this, you can file a complaint with the Attorney General, who must set up a complaint site. Flag for review: from 2027-07-01, may preempt Jersey City Code § 218-12 (Ord. 25-057, as amended by Ord. 25-076).

Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. If you were overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you out of any penalty collected. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U" (rule covers 3+).)

Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, with notice periods ranging from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, your landlord cannot raise your rent to cover costs that result solely from the conversion. Rent may still rise to pay for new services or amenities. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the building is being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership.)

Applies. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your source of lawful income, such as a housing voucher. You can file a complaint with the NJ Division of Civil Rights or in Superior Court. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. A New Jersey landlord cannot ask about your criminal record, orally or on an application, until after making you a conditional offer, except about methamphetamine production on federally assisted premises or lifetime sex-offender registration. You may give the landlord evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. Before taking any application fee, a New Jersey landlord must tell you in writing whether it reviews criminal history. It must also tell you that you may give evidence of errors in your record or of rehabilitation. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Even after a conditional offer, a New Jersey landlord may never consider arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U", so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Jersey City landlords and their agents may not pay for or contract with a 'service provider' that pools competitors' nonpublic rent, supply or occupancy data and uses software to recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy levels. Service providers may not facilitate agreements among landlords not to compete on rents, fees or other terms. Tenants can report suspected use to the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations or sue if harmed. Note: Ordinance text calls Chapter 218 both 'Multiple Dwellings' and 'Fees and Charges', and renumbers existing §§ 218-12 through 218-18; codified section number should be verified. Effective date is computed, not stated. Flag for review: from 2027-07-01, possible conflict with Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act – ban on algorithmic rent coordination (N.J.S.A. 56:9-20 to 56:9-26 (P.L. 2026, c.43; A3497 ACS 1R)).

Applies. If you rent in a Jersey City building with 5 or more units, your rent may be regulated under the city's Rent Control Ordinance. You can ask the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations about your building's status through SeeClickFix or file an Illegal Rent Petition if you think your rent is illegal. (21 units, from the assessor class code "4S-B-A-21U" (rule covers 5+).)

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. In Newark rent-controlled units, rent may not rise more than the allowed percentage in any 12-month period, and never more than 4%, even if tenants or owners change. No increase is allowed if the building is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered the unit, so check the registration with the Office of Rent Control.

May apply (the building's age is not in the data). If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. It only applies if the owner filed the required notice, which public data can't show.

A0327.explanation: Applies. Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

Applies. A landlord may charge an application screening fee no higher than the actual out-of-pocket cost of screening you, and never more than $30 per applicant, adjusted annually for CPI increases since 1998. Ask for the current CPI-adjusted figure if you are charged more than $30. A landlord may not charge you a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A landlord may charge a screening fee only if they either consider complete applications in order received under written criteria (approving the first qualified applicant and charging only when your application is actually considered, refunding within 7 days if collected by mistake), or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever is first. The landlord must give you an itemized receipt (in person, by mail, or by email if agreed) showing out-of-pocket costs and time spent, and must return any part of the fee not used if no reference check or credit report was obtained. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your consumer credit report within seven days of receiving it, by personal delivery, mail, or email.

Covered, but superseded here: No eviction for nonpayment unless arrears exceed Fair Market Rent (L.A. Mun. Code §§ 151.09(A)(1), 165.03(A) (Ord. No. 187763)) governs this address. Once all tenants have lawfully lived in the unit for 12 months (or at least one tenant for 24 months), your landlord may evict only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written termination notice. For a curable lease violation, the landlord must first give you a notice and a chance to fix it. If your landlord ends a covered tenancy for a no-fault reason (owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel), they must either pay you one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 calendar days of the notice or waive your final month's rent in writing. The notice must tell you about this right; if the landlord does not strictly comply, the notice is void.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower).) Note: Stated on a city agency's page (Los Angeles, CA), not in the state's own text; check the figure against an official state source.

Covered, but superseded here: Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) annual allowable rent increase (L.A. Mun. Code § 151.06 (annual increase, as amended by Ord. No. 188795), § 151.02 (Rent Stabilization Ordinance)) governs this address. For a covered unit, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus local CPI, or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, measured from the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months. If you stay in the unit, the rent can be raised no more than twice in 12 months, and the landlord can set any starting rent for a new tenancy.

Applies. A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history. (36 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 1 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed. (36 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. In an RSO unit, your landlord can evict only for a listed reason. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, lease violations, nuisance, or illegal use. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, a resident manager, demolition, a government order, or conversion to affordable housing. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict, give 30- or 60-day notice (sometimes 120 days), and pay relocation assistance. All termination notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days. (built 1954, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for a no-fault reason (owner or relative move-in, demolition or removal from rental use, government order to vacate, conversion, and similar), the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. The landlord must also pay you relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice; the 2026-27 amounts run from $11,000 to $27,400 depending on your tenancy length, income, age, disability or children. If you are not paid, you can raise the non-payment as a defense to the eviction and file a complaint with LAHD. (36 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.) Note: Bulletin A says a copy of the termination notice must be filed with LAHD no later than 3 days after service, while Bulletin B says within 3 business days. The fee chart in Bulletin B is labeled effective July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, while Bulletin A labels the same fees July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027.

Applies. If you rent in Los Angeles in a unit not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance and have lived there at least six months (or your original lease has expired), your landlord can evict you only for a listed at-fault or no-fault reason. For no-fault reasons, such as an owner move-in, demolition or removal from the rental market, the landlord may have to pay you relocation assistance.
Applies. In Los Angeles RSO and JCO units, your landlord cannot evict you for falling behind on rent unless you owe more than one month's Fair Market Rent for your unit's bedroom size.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your unit is a Protected Unit (this includes all RSO units) and is being demolished for new construction, you are entitled to at least the RSO/JCO relocation amount. If your household is lower income, you get the higher RPO or state amounts, up to $115,480 for extremely low income households under the City's standardized option. RPO protections also include a 6-month notice, a right to stay until 6 months before construction starts, a right to return if demolition does not proceed, and for some tenants a right of first refusal in the new building. (Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether a non-RSO unit is a Protected Unit (affordability covenant, occupancy by lower-income households within 5 years, or Ellis withdrawal within 10 years); Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Whether the unit is being demolished for new construction; Unknown: coverage requires a fact not in the data: Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower) for enhanced payments.)

Applies. If your LA unit was first built on or before October 1, 1978, your landlord may raise rent only once every 12 months, by no more than the city's published allowable percentage. Since February 2, 2026, landlords cannot add an extra percentage for utilities or a 10% increase for an added dependent. Increases beyond this, such as for capital improvements, need LAHD approval. (built 1954, before the 1978-10-01 cutoff.) Note: D042: Sources disagree: status in_force; effective date 2025-07-01 / 2026-02-02.

Applies. If you rent an RSO unit in Los Angeles (certificate of occupancy first issued before October 1, 1978) and your landlord has held your deposit for at least a year, the landlord must pay you interest (3.03% for 2026, or the actual interest earned with a bank statement), as a direct payment or rent credit, and any unpaid interest when you move out. If unpaid, you can sue, including in Small Claims Court; the city will not investigate. (built 1954, before the 1978-09-30 cutoff.)

It may consider only listed serious convictions, first-degree offenses within 6 years, second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years, and fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must give written reasons and an individualized assessment, and you may request within 30 days, free of charge, all the information it relied on. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. Your landlord cannot collect a security deposit (including any pet deposit or prepaid last month's rent) of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit cannot exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends, or you can sue for double the amount wrongly withheld. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

May apply. New construction can be exempt from local rent control for 30 years under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.2 (P.L.1987, c.153) if the owner filed a notice, and here the building's age is not in the data. In Newark rent-controlled units, rent may not rise more than the allowed percentage in any 12-month period, and never more than 4%, even if tenants or owners change. No increase is allowed if the building is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered the unit, so check the registration with the Office of Rent Control.

May apply (the building's age is not in the data). If your building is a newly constructed multiple dwelling, it is exempt from local rent control for 30 years after construction is completed. Check with your rent control board or municipal clerk to confirm whether your unit is covered. It only applies if the owner filed the required notice, which public data can't show.

Applies. The landlord must give you an itemized receipt (in person, by mail, or by email if agreed) showing out-of-pocket costs and time spent, and must return any part of the fee not used if no reference check or credit report was obtained. Applies. Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed. (24 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. If your landlord evicts you for a no-fault reason (owner or relative move-in, demolition or removal from rental use, government order to vacate, conversion, and similar), the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. The landlord must also pay you relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice; the 2026-27 amounts run from $11,000 to $27,400 depending on your tenancy length, income, age, disability or children. If you are not paid, you can raise the non-payment as a defense to the eviction and file a complaint with LAHD. (24 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 4 units) cannot apply.) Applies. If you rent in Los Angeles in a unit not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance and have lived there at least six months (or your original lease has expired), your landlord can evict you only for a listed at-fault or no-fault reason. Applies. In Los Angeles RSO and JCO units, your landlord cannot evict you for falling behind on rent unless you owe more than one month's Fair Market Rent for your unit's bedroom size.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your unit is a Protected Unit (this includes all RSO units) and is being demolished for new construction, you are entitled to at least the RSO/JCO relocation amount. RPO protections also include a 6-month notice, a right to stay until 6 months before construction starts, a right to return if demolition does not proceed, and for some tenants a right of first refusal in the new building. Applies. A landlord or its agent cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted yearly for inflation starting January 1, 2027) as an application or similar fee to apply to rent or sublease a home. Applies. Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease (written or oral) without one of the good causes listed in the Anti-Eviction Act, proven in court. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance equal to six times the monthly rent. (at least 5 units, inferred from New Jersey property class 4C, which state law defines as property for 5 or more families, so the owner-type exemption (up to 3 units) cannot apply.)

Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but your rent cannot be raised mid-lease, and any increase requires a proper notice to quit and an offer of a new lease. The increase must not be unconscionable and must follow any local rent control ordinance. Ask your municipal rent control board or clerk whether your unit is covered.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. Applies. In Massachusetts, a rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who originally hired and contracted with the broker. If the landlord hired the broker, you as a tenant cannot be made to pay that fee.

Applies. At or before move-in, a landlord or the landlord's agent can only require you to pay first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of up to one month's rent, and the cost of a new lock and key. Since August 1, 2025, this also bars requiring you to pay the landlord's agent (such as the landlord's broker) anything beyond those items.

Applies. A landlord who threatens or takes reprisals (including eviction notices, rent increases or changed lease terms) because you complained about code violations, took legal action, or joined a tenants' union owes you at least one to three months' rent or your actual damages plus attorney's fees. A termination notice (other than for nonpayment), rent increase or substantial change in terms within six months after such activity is presumed to be retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence.

Applies. Massachusetts cities and towns generally cannot enact, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no local rent cap to rely on. The only exception is a voluntary program for owners of 10 or more units with fair market rent of $400 or less, where the city pays owners the difference from its general funds.

Applies. A Massachusetts landlord may not refuse to rent to you or otherwise discriminate against you because you receive public assistance or a housing subsidy such as a rental voucher, or because of that program's requirements. Ads may not state a preference against public assistance recipients.

Applies. Your landlord cannot charge a security deposit larger than one month's rent, must put it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and must give you a signed statement of the apartment's condition. If the state housing office issues regulations, a landlord may offer an optional fee in lieu of a deposit, and deposit plus fees can never exceed one month's rent in total. Your landlord must return your security deposit, minus only unpaid rent/water charges, allowed tax escalation, or documented damage beyond normal wear and tear, within 30 days after you move out, and must pay you yearly interest on it. If the landlord fails to return it on time, you can sue for three times the amount owed plus court costs and attorney's fees.

Applies. Any Boston landlord planning to end your tenancy must give you a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources together with the Notice to Quit or non-renewal notice; if you didn't get it, report it to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity (617-635-2500 or 311). A violation does not stop the eviction process. Note: Notice requirement only; Boston, MA has no just-cause eviction law.

May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. May apply; the public data cannot settle coverage. If your landlord ends your tenancy for a no-fault reason, they must pay you two months of your current rent (three months if you are a senior aged 62 or older, or disabled), regardless of your income or length of tenancy. The landlord may instead waive the same amount of rent, and must pay a direct payment within 15 days of the notice. (8 units, so the owner-type exemption (up to 2 units) cannot apply; Unknown: buildings newer than 15 years are exempt, and the year built is not in the data.)

Applies. A San Diego landlord may not refuse to rent or renew, end a tenancy, falsely say a unit is unavailable, or advertise a preference based on your source of income, which includes Section 8 and other rental, deposit, or homeless assistance. Any income standard must count all of your income, including assistance, plus the combined income of co-tenants and cosigners.

Applies. A Berkeley landlord cannot charge an existing tenant a non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy or to add, replace, or remove a roommate. Lease terms to the contrary are unenforceable.
